section.title: The Kings Defeated
section.sectionRationale: The conquest narrative closes with a roll call of victory. Chapter 12 lists the kings defeated on both sides of the Jordan: those Moses struck down in the east, and the thirty-one kings Joshua struck down in the west. It is one movement, a summary catalog that stands as a monument to what God has done, marking the transition from the taking of the land to its division among the tribes.
section.thesis: The long list of conquered kings is a testimony, not a boast: every name records a promise kept and a victory God gave, so that the whole roll, thirty-one kings on the west and two great kings on the east, stands as a memorial to the faithfulness of the God who gave His people the land.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the two kings defeated east of the Jordan under Moses, verses 1 to 6; and the thirty-one kings defeated west of the Jordan under Joshua, verses 7 to 24.

units.label: The kings defeated east of the Jordan
units.note: Sihon and Og, struck down under Moses

verses.text: Now these are the {{melek|kings}} of the land whom the Israelites struck down and whose lands they {{yarash|took}} beyond the Jordan to the east, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including all the Arabah eastward:

Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. He ruled from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along the middle of the valley, up to the Jabbok River (the border of the Ammonites), that is, half of Gilead,
as well as the Arabah east of the Sea of Chinnereth to the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea), eastward through Beth-jeshimoth, and southward below the slopes of Pisgah.
And Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei.
He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah, all of Bashan up to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and half of Gilead to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon.
Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the Israelites had struck them down and given their land as an {{nachalah|inheritance}} to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

units.label: The thirty-one kings defeated west of the Jordan
units.note: so there were thirty-one kings in all

verses.text: And these are the kings of the land that Joshua and the Israelites conquered beyond the Jordan to the west, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir (according to the allotments to the tribes of Israel, Joshua gave them as an inheritance
the hill country, the foothills, the Arabah, the slopes, the wilderness, and the Negev, the lands of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites):
the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is near Bethel, one;
the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;
the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;
the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;
the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;
the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;
the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;
the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;
the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;
the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;
the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;
the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;
the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;
the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Gilgal, one;
and the king of Tirzah, one. So there were thirty-one kings in all.

melek.gloss: King, ruler. Canaan was a patchwork of independent city-states, each with its own melek; the roll of thirty-one kings shows how fragmented and yet how heavily fortified the land was. Every named king is a power that stood against the LORD and fell, so the list magnifies the God who is King over all kings and gives them into His people's hand.

yarash.gloss: To take possession of, dispossess, inherit. The Israelites yarash the lands of the defeated kings, the key conquest verb that holds together gift and effort: the land is God's to give, yet it is entered and possessed as the enemy is dispossessed. The catalog records the outworking of that possession across the whole land, east and west.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession. The conquered land becomes the tribes' nachalah, a heritage given by God rather than seized by right. The word bridges this summary of conquest into the coming chapters of allotment, where the inheritance is carefully divided; every king's fall clears the way for a tribe's inherited portion.

basic.context: Chapter 12 is a summary, a victory list that closes the story of the conquest before the book turns to dividing the land. It has two parts. First it recalls the two kings defeated east of the Jordan under Moses, Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, whose lands became the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Then it lists the thirty-one kings Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, city by city, from Jericho and Ai to the great northern centers, ending with the total: thirty-one kings in all. It may read like a dry catalog, but it is really a monument. Each name is a fortress that fell and a promise God kept. The question underneath is: how do we rightly remember and give thanks for what God has done?
basic.hermeneutics: This is a summary list within historical narrative, and its function is memorial and transitional. Lists like this are easy to skim, but in Scripture they often serve to record God's faithfulness in concrete detail. The chapter ties Moses' victories and Joshua's together, showing continuity in God's work, and it prepares for the allotment of the land. We read it not for battle tactics but as a testimony to a promise fully kept.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter counts the melek, the kings, each city-state's ruler, thirty-one in the west plus two great kings in the east. Israel yarash, takes possession of, their lands. And the conquered territory becomes the tribes' nachalah, their inheritance by gift.
basic.typology: The roll of defeated kings points forward to Christ, the King of kings, before whom every earthly power will finally fall, and to the inheritance secured for God's people. The uniting of Moses' and Joshua's victories pictures the one saving work of God carried through His servants and completed in Christ.
basic.christ: Every king in this list stood against the LORD and fell; the catalog anticipates the day when every rule and authority is put under the feet of Christ, the King of kings and Lord of lords, Revelation 19:16. And the inheritance these victories secured points to the eternal inheritance won for God's people in Him.
basic.god: God is the great King who gives kings into His people's hand and fulfills His promises down to the last detail. He is faithful across generations, from Moses to Joshua. And He is the giver of the inheritance, clearing every obstacle so His people may possess what He swore to their fathers.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 21 records the defeat of Sihon and Og under Moses. Deuteronomy 3 recalls those eastern victories. Psalm 136 gives thanks that God struck down mighty kings, for His steadfast love endures forever. And Revelation 19 names Christ King of kings, before whom every ruler falls.
basic.oneStory: The catalog of defeated kings is a monument to God's faithfulness, recording every promise kept as the land is taken east and west. It closes the conquest and opens the way to the inheritance, and it points forward to Christ, the King of kings, before whom every power will fall and in whom God's people receive their lasting inheritance.

context.literary:
Chapter 12 forms a deliberate envelope with Joshua 11:16 to 23. That earlier paragraph narrates the whole campaign in summary prose, "so Joshua took the whole land," and ends "then the land had rest from war." Chapter 12 answers it with a formal register that turns the same conquest into a countable catalogue. The unit divides cleanly in two: verses 1 to 6 gather the eastern victories under Moses into six verses of connected narrative prose, while verses 7 to 24 compress thirty-one western victories into a bare, repetitive list, the king of Jericho, one, the king of Ai, one, continuing without further comment until the closing tally.

The genre shift matters. The opening formula, these are the kings of the land, announces a discrete literary unit, the kind of heading that elsewhere in Scripture marks a change of subject, and the numbering after each name functions like a scribe's tally mark rather than a narrated event; nothing is said of how any individual king fell, because the chapter's interest is cumulative, not episodic. The list's order roughly traces the campaigns already narrated, opening in the south at Jericho and Ai and closing in the north at Hazor and Tirzah, so an attentive reader recognizes almost the whole itinerary of chapters 6 to 11 compressed into eighteen verses.

The chapter therefore functions as a hinge: it closes the conquest section by turning narrated victory into an official record, and its double note about inheritance in verses 6 and 7 opens directly onto the allotment chapters that follow.
context.historical:
Late Bronze Age Canaan was never a single kingdom. Egyptian records from this same era describe the land as a crowded quilt of small city-kingdoms, each with its own ruler contesting its neighbors, exactly the situation this list assumes when it can count thirty-one separate kings ruling within one relatively small stretch of territory. Cities named here, Megiddo, Hazor, Gezer, Lachish, Jerusalem, were substantial fortified centers by the standards of the age, some among the largest in the southern Levant, so the scale of victory the chapter records is over walled strongholds with standing garrisons, not undefended villages.

Sihon and Og, the two eastern kings, belonged to an older campaign remembered independently in Israel's national memory. Sihon had himself displaced the Moabites from territory north of the Arnon, and Og, described as one of the remnant of the Rephaim, was associated in popular memory with the same vanishing race of giants that also produced the Emites among the Moabites and the Zamzummites among the Ammonites, so that Deuteronomy preserves the detail of his enormous iron bed kept as a curiosity at Rabbah long afterward.

The list's geography is exact rather than impressionistic. Verses 1 to 5 trace real administrative boundaries, the Arnon, the Jabbok, Mount Hermon, of the kind later Iron Age inscriptions from the region continue to use, which is part of why catalogues like this functioned as genuine territorial records in the ancient Near East rather than literary flourish.
context.canonical:
The chapter's two kings under Moses and thirty-one under Joshua are never treated as separate achievements elsewhere in Scripture; they are folded into a single testimony to one God acting through two servants. Psalm 136 is the clearest example: its refrain, His loving devotion endures forever, is sung over Sihon and Og by name in the very same breath as the exodus and the wilderness, showing that Israel's worship did not distinguish Moses' victories from Joshua's as separate mercies but as one continuous account of covenant faithfulness.

Joshua 21:44 to 45, closing the whole first half of the book, supplies the theological headline this catalogue only implies: the LORD gave Israel rest on every side, and not one of His good promises had failed. Chapter 12's roll of names is the evidence; chapter 21 supplies the verdict.

The listing of thirty-one city-kings also anticipates a recurring biblical pattern in which the multiplication of small, defeated rulers becomes shorthand for total victory, most fully in the New Testament's vision of every dominion, authority, and power finally destroyed and every king bowing to the one on whom the title King of kings is written. Even the phrase the kings of the land reappears with theological weight later in the historical books, where Israel's own request for a king like the nations will complicate this earlier picture of the LORD alone deposing every rival king; chapter 12 stands as an early, uncomplicated instance of the theme before Israel's own monarchy raises its own questions about kingship.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author's aim is closer to that of a scribe compiling an official record than a storyteller adding a new episode: nothing happens in chapter 12 that has not already happened in chapters 2 through 11, and that repetition is the point. By naming every fallen king in one place, the compiler invites Israel to read its recent history as a single, itemized ledger of divine faithfulness rather than a string of separate battles remembered piecemeal.

Uniting Moses' two eastern victories with Joshua's thirty-one western ones under one heading also serves a covenantal purpose. It insists that the conquest is one continuous act of the LORD carried out through successive leaders, so that no future generation could set the memory of Moses against the memory of Joshua, or credit the western victories to Joshua's generalship apart from the same God who gave Sihon and Og into Israel's hand a generation earlier.

The placement of this list immediately before the allotment chapters signals a further intent: before any tribe receives a boundary line, the reader must first see, city by city, that the total territory God promised has, in fact, been delivered into Israel's hand.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nothing in this chapter issues a command; it is pure historical description, a tally of what God had already done, and no reader is asked to conquer thirty-one cities or replicate a military campaign. Its abiding value lies in the practice it models rather than in any instruction it gives: Israel is shown counting and naming its mercies rather than letting them blur into vague gratitude.

That habit of specific remembrance is transferable even though the specific victories are not. A modern reader keeps no list of defeated Canaanite kings, but the passage still commends the discipline of naming, in detail, what God has actually done, rather than resting in generalized thanks.

It is worth noting what the chapter does not claim. It never says every inhabitant of the land was removed, nor does it promise perpetual, uncontested peace; the very next chapter opens by admitting how much land remains to be possessed, a reminder that this catalogue records real victories within a still unfinished story, not a final, static conquest.

debates.question: Why include such a granular, repetitive list of thirty-one names instead of a summary sentence?

views.label: A tally deliberately built for cumulative effect
views.case: The bare repetition, one, one, one, is rhetorical, not merely administrative. Modern readers skim lists, but ancient hearers receiving this aloud would have felt the weight accumulate with every name, so that the plain, unadorned form itself preaches total, comprehensive victory more forcefully than a summary count could.

views.label: An administrative record with a real, verifiable function
views.case: The list also served a practical purpose contemporary with the events themselves, recording exactly which conquered territories were available for allotment. It functions less like a psalm and more like a land registry, and its dry style is exactly what a legal record requires, not a flaw to be explained away.

debates.bearing: Both functions can be true together: the list's plain administrative form is precisely what allows it to double as an unanswerable testimony, since a fabricated or exaggerated victory claim would need embellishment, while a real accounting needs none.

debates.question: Does grouping Sihon and Og with the thirty-one western kings imply their conquest was equal in kind, or different?

views.label: One continuous work, different only in leader
views.case: The chapter's single heading over both halves, and its explicit statement that Moses struck them down exactly as Joshua did the western kings, argues that Scripture treats the two campaigns as one work under two servants, resisting any reader's temptation to rank Joshua's conquest above Moses' or treat the earlier victories as a lesser precursor.

views.label: Two distinct grants reflecting two distinct calls
views.case: The eastern land was requested by Reuben and Gad for their cattle and granted somewhat provisionally before the main crossing, Numbers 32:33, while the western land was allotted only after the full nation crossed the Jordan under the covenant sign of circumcision at Gilgal, so the chapter's two-part structure preserves a real difference in how each grant came about even while affirming that the same God gave both.

debates.bearing: The chapter's own structure supports the first reading over the second: whatever differences attended how each grant arose, the text refuses to separate the theology of the two conquests, uniting them under a single formula and a single tally so that both are received the same way, as gift.

study.originalLanguages:
Two small grammatical details, easy to miss in English, carry real weight in this chapter. First, the verb translated struck down throughout, nakah, is the ordinary Hebrew verb for a decisive, often fatal blow; it is the same verb used of the plagues that struck Egypt and of David's blow against Goliath, so its repetition across both halves of the chapter, of Moses in verse 6 and of Joshua in verse 7, quietly binds the two conquests into one continuous action by the same divine hand, rather than two campaigns that merely resemble each other.

Second, the western half of the list is built almost entirely on a single recurring word, one, echad, attached to every king's name, the king of Jericho, one, and so on, thirty-one times. English can only render this with a number after a semicolon, but in Hebrew it functions as a spoken tally, a scribe or a worshiper counting off victories aloud one at a time. The device turns a list that could have been a single summarizing sentence into something closer to a liturgy of remembrance, each king's fall marked individually before the final total is given.

A third detail sits in the directional phrasing of verses 1 and 7. Both describe territory beyond the Jordan, using the same underlying phrase, but the chapter is careful to add a second word to remove the ambiguity: verse 1 specifies to the east, and verse 7 specifies to the west. The phrase by itself simply meant the region across the river and could point either direction depending on where the speaker stood; Moses, describing the land from the east bank before Israel crossed, and the later record arranging this chapter from a settled, western vantage point, both needed the extra directional word to keep readers oriented, a small textual fingerprint of a record compiled after Israel had settled on both sides of the river.

Finally, Og is called one of the remnant of the Rephaim, a term the Old Testament also uses of the enormous, half-legendary populations Israel's own spies feared in Numbers 13, and which Deuteronomy 2 associates with peoples known locally by other names, the Emites among the Moabites and the Zamzummites among the Ammonites. The label functions less as an ethnic classification than as a marker of formidable size and ancient reputation: to say Og was Rephaim told an Israelite audience immediately why his defeat mattered so much, and why his iron bed was still a curiosity worth remembering generations later, Deuteronomy 3:11.

typology.type: The roll of thirty-one kings brought low before the LORD
typology.fulfillment: Every earthly throne in Canaan fell in one campaign, foreshadowing the day when, as Paul writes, Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet, and hands the kingdom to the Father, having destroyed every dominion, authority, and power, 1 Corinthians 15:24-25. Revelation pictures the same reality completed: the rider whose name is King of kings and Lord of lords subdues the kings of the earth themselves, Revelation 19:16. The type intensifies rather than merely repeats: Joshua's kings lost only territory and life, while the powers Christ defeats include death itself, the last enemy to be destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

typology.type: The inheritance secured once every rival king had fallen
typology.fulfillment: Only after every contesting king was struck down could the land in verses 6 and 7 become an inheritance for the tribes; the pattern anticipates an inheritance secured only after every hostile power is subdued. Peter describes it as imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven, 1 Peter 1:4, and Paul calls the Spirit the pledge of that inheritance until believers take full possession, Ephesians 1:13-14. The type deepens here too: Canaan could still be lost to unfaithfulness, as later history shows, while the inheritance kept for believers in Christ cannot be forfeited, only awaited.

typology.type: Moses' and Joshua's victories gathered as one continuous work
typology.fulfillment: The chapter refuses to separate what Moses began from what Joshua finished, crediting both to the LORD who acted through each in turn. Hebrews draws the same line further, comparing Moses, faithful as a servant in God's house, to Christ, faithful as a Son over that house, Hebrews 3:5-6, and describing every faithful figure of the old covenant as commended for faith yet not receiving what was promised until God provided something better, together with us, Hebrews 11:39-40. The type's limit is plain: Moses and Joshua each completed a partial stage of one plan; only Christ completes it entirely, needing no successor to finish His work.

study.christ:
Joshua's own name is where this chapter's typology begins, though the chapter itself never comments on it. Yehoshua, the LORD saves, is the very name later rendered in Greek as Jesus. The man under whom thirty-one fortified kings fell bears, in Hebrew, the name the angel tells Joseph to give Mary's son, because he will save his people from their sins, Matthew 1:21. Scripture is not shy about drawing the line itself: Hebrews notes that if Joshua had given Israel final rest, God would not have spoken of another day later, implying that Joshua's conquest, real as it was, was never meant to be the last word, Hebrews 4:8-9. This chapter's catalogue, in other words, is not a completed victory to imitate so much as an unfinished sentence waiting for its true subject.

The chapter's arithmetic points the same direction. Thirty-one kings, named and tallied, none surviving, foreshadow a far larger reckoning: Paul says the Son must reign until He has put every enemy under His feet, and names death itself as the last one destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26. Where Joshua's list closes with a number, Colossians closes the greater version with an image, Christ stripping rulers and authorities of their power and putting them on open display, triumphing over them by the cross, Colossians 2:15. The defeated kings of Canaan lost only cities; the powers Christ defeats at Calvary held humanity itself captive.

Even the eastern half of the list, Sihon and Og under Moses rather than Joshua, has its own quiet pointer. Hebrews compares Moses, faithful as a servant within God's house, to Christ, faithful as a Son over that house, a comparison this very chapter makes almost inevitable by placing Moses' victories and Joshua's side by side as one continuous work, Hebrews 3:5-6. The two servants together prepare for a greater one, a Son who does not merely serve within the house of a promised land and defeated kings but reigns over the far larger house of every people whose allegiance is His, Genesis 49:10 and Revelation 5:5. What chapter 12 records in miniature and in the past tense, the New Testament announces in full and as a future certainty: every king will fall, and one King alone will remain standing.
study.god:
This chapter never uses the word holy or just, yet both truths sit underneath every line of it. Ancient Canaanite religion cast its kings as representatives, sometimes even titled sons, of gods like Baal and Asherah who were believed to guarantee the land's fertility and the city's safety; the fall of thirty-one such kings before the LORD is therefore not merely a change of government but a catalogue proving that the gods behind those thrones had no power to save their own. Chapter 12 is a quiet answer to every rival claim to ultimate authority in the land: none of it held.

God's care in this record is also exact rather than sweeping. He is not praised here in the abstract for giving victory; every single king is named, every territory described down to its boundary markers, as though the God who receives credit refuses to let His faithfulness be summarized away into vague generalities. A God who counts to thirty-one, and remembers each city by name, is a God who deals in particulars, not impressions.

The chapter also holds together patience and resolve in a way easy to miss. Decades separate Moses' two eastern victories from Joshua's western thirty-one, yet both are gathered under one roof as a single act, which means God was never in a hurry to complete what He had promised, nor did the long gap between the two campaigns weaken His resolve to finish it.

And nothing in the chapter suggests indiscriminate violence: the same God who commands the defeat of these particular fortified, war-making city-kings is the God who in the surrounding chapters spares Rahab, receives the Gibeonites, and will soon give the tribe of Levi no land but Himself, Joshua 13:14 and 33. Judgment on entrenched, idolatrous kingship and mercy toward those who turn to Him are two sides of the same holy character, never in tension in the text itself.

crossReferences.note: This passage narrates in real time what Joshua 12 only tallies: Sihon refusing Israel safe passage, gathering his army at Jahaz, and falling to the sword, after which Israel occupied his cities outright. The catalogue in Joshua compresses an entire campaign, complete with its own victory song about Heshbon, into a single summarizing verse.

Moses' own retelling adds detail the tally omits: Og's army met Israel at Edrei, all sixty of his fortified cities fell without exception, and his massive iron bed remained on display at Rabbah long afterward. The detail of the bed shows how long Israelites kept telling this particular story before Joshua 12 folded it into a single line.

Moses had already given the conquered territory of Sihon and Og to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh before Israel ever crossed the Jordan, the very grant that Joshua 12:6 recalls. The two passages together show one continuous act of allotment spanning a full generation and two leaders.

Israel's temple worship set this same catalogue to music, naming Sihon and Og specifically inside a refrain about the LORD's enduring loving devotion. Singing the names of defeated kings rather than only the fact of victory turned Joshua 12's dry record into an act of praise repeated for generations.

The verdict this whole catalogue has been building toward arrives at the close of the conquest section: the LORD gave Israel rest on every side, and not one of His good promises had failed. Chapter 12's roll of names is the evidence; chapter 21 supplies the summary verdict.

Paul takes the pattern of chapter 12, many rulers subdued one by one, and applies it to the whole of history: Christ must reign until every dominion, authority, and power is destroyed, with death named as the last enemy to fall. Joshua's tally of thirty-one is a small, early instance of a far larger reckoning.

Where Joshua 12 records earthly kings struck down in battle, Paul describes a cosmic version of the same event at the cross, where Christ disarmed rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them. The defeated kings of Canaan lost cities; the powers Christ defeated held humanity captive.

The chapter's own move, treating Moses' eastern victories and Joshua's western ones as one continuous work, anticipates this comparison: Moses was faithful as a servant within God's house, but Christ is faithful as a Son over that house. Two servants prepare the way for one greater Son.

Joshua's Hebrew name, meaning the LORD saves, is the very name later given in Greek form, Jesus, to Mary's son, because he would save his people from their sins. The man under whom thirty-one kings fell carries, in his own name, a pointer to a far greater deliverance.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 gave humanity dominion over creation as vice-regents under God; by Genesis 3 that dominion was fractured, and by the time of Abraham the land meant for blessing lay instead under the rule of hostile kings, five of whom Abraham himself once had to rescue Lot from, Genesis 14:1-16. Joshua 12 answers that long history of contested rule with a plain, countable reversal: every throne raised against the LORD's purposes in this land, thirty-one in the west and two great ones in the east, has fallen. It is a small but real down payment on the promise given to Abraham that his offspring would possess the gate of their enemies, Genesis 22:17.

The chapter also sits at a hinge in the unfolding plan. Behind it lies the exodus and forty years of wilderness testing that this very catalogue only obliquely recalls, Sihon and Og struck down at the very edge of the promised land, the last obstacle before Israel could even begin the western conquest. Ahead of it lies the allotment, in which this reclaimed territory becomes each tribe's inheritance, and further still lies Israel's own request for a king, when the nation that watched thirty-one foreign kings fall will itself ask for a king like the nations, a request Samuel warns against and God nonetheless permits, 1 Samuel 8:5-7. The catalogue of chapter 12 marks a victory that Israel's own future kingship will not always live up to.

The whole trajectory bends toward a King who never disappoints that hope. What chapter 12 records as completed and past, one land fully subdued, the New Testament describes as certain but not yet consummated: every rule and authority still awaits its final destruction, 1 Corinthians 15:24, and the earth still awaits the day the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, Revelation 11:15. Joshua 12 is a chapter-length rehearsal, in miniature, of history's whole shape: dominion lost, dominion partially reclaimed by promise, and dominion finally and forever secured in the Son of David who is also, in name, the greater Joshua.

options.text: A summary list of all the kings Israel defeated, east under Moses and west under Joshua.
options.note: The chapter catalogs the conquered kings on both sides of the Jordan as a memorial of victory.

options.text: A detailed account of a single new battle.
options.note: It summarizes many past victories rather than narrating one new battle.

options.text: A list of the tribes and their leaders.
options.note: It lists defeated kings, not the tribes and their leaders.
It is a catalog of defeated kings, not a collection of prayers.

quiz.q: Which two great kings east of the Jordan does the chapter recall, and under whom did they fall?

options.text: Sihon and Og, defeated under Moses, whose land went to the eastern tribes.
options.note: Verses 2 to 6 recall Sihon and Og struck down under Moses.

options.text: Adoni-zedek and Jabin, defeated under Joshua.
options.note: Those kings fell under Joshua in the west; the eastern kings recalled here are Sihon and Og under Moses.

options.text: The kings of Jericho and Ai, defeated under Moses.
options.note: Jericho and Ai fell under Joshua in the west; the eastern kings were Sihon and Og under Moses.

options.text: No kings are mentioned east of the Jordan.
options.note: Sihon and Og are specifically named as the eastern kings defeated under Moses.

quiz.q: How many kings did Joshua defeat west of the Jordan?

options.note: Verse 24 gives the total, thirty-one kings, a tally of comprehensive victory.

options.text: Exactly seven kings, one for each nation.
options.note: There were seven nations, but thirty-one individual city-kings were defeated.
Sihon and Og fell in the east under Moses; the western total under Joshua was thirty-one.
The stated total is thirty-one kings, not over a hundred.

quiz.q: Why does Scripture include such a detailed catalog of kings and cities?

options.text: As a memorial to God's complete faithfulness, recording that not one of His promises failed.
options.note: The list is a concrete testimony that God kept His promise to give the land, city by city.

options.text: To brag about Israel's military genius.
options.note: The list testifies to God's faithfulness, not Israel's genius; the victories are credited to the LORD.

options.text: To provide directions for future travelers.
options.note: It is a memorial of conquest, not a travel guide.

options.text: For no particular reason; it is filler.
options.note: The catalog is a deliberate memorial of God's faithfulness and a bridge to the allotment of the land.

questions: The list turns victory into a written memorial. What specific answers to prayer or acts of God's faithfulness could you write down and keep as your own record of what He has done?
Every named king was a power that fell before the LORD. What seemingly immovable obstacle in your life do you need to trust to the God who brings down kings?
The chapter joins Moses' victories to Joshua's as one work of God. How does it encourage you to see God working consistently across different seasons and leaders in your own life and church?
The fallen kings point to Christ, the King of kings, under whom every power will finally bow. How does that future certainty shape the way you face opposition now?
The conquered land became the tribes' inheritance. How does the promise of an imperishable inheritance in Christ steady you when earthly things feel uncertain?

translationNotes.note: The Sea of Chinnereth is the Sea of Galilee, and the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, is the Dead Sea, as the BSB footnotes note.

The BSB footnote notes that the Septuagint reads Og king of Bashan, while the Hebrew reads the territory of Og king of Bashan; Og is noted as one of the last of the Rephaim, a people of great stature.
